claim: Too many partition keys fragment a dataset into too many small files, while too few partition keys or none at all make queries scan more data than necessary.
question: What goes wrong with too many or too few partition keys in Athena?

values.display: too many files and files that are too small
queries that scan more data than necessary

evidence.quote: Having too many partition keys can result in fragmented datasets with too many files and files that are too small. Conversely, having too few partition keys, or no partitioning at all, leads to queries that scan more data than necessary.

claim: Optimize partitioning for the most common queries and not for rare ones. If queries look at time spans of days, do not partition by hour.
question: How fine should Athena time partitions be?

values.display: optimize for the most common queries
don't partition by hour

qualifiers.condition: queries look at time spans of days

evidence.quote: A good strategy is to optimize for the most common queries and avoid optimizing for rare queries. For example, if your queries look at time spans of days, don't partition by hour, even if some queries filter to that level.

claim: Partition indexes are an AWS Glue Data Catalog feature that improves partition lookup performance for tables with large numbers of partitions.
question: What improves partition lookup for Athena tables with very many partitions?

values.display: improves partition lookup performance
tables that have large numbers of partitions

evidence.quote: Partition indexes are a feature in the AWS Glue Data Catalog that improves partition lookup performance for tables that have large numbers of partitions.

claim: Athena requires partition keys to be of type STRING to push down partition filtering into AWS Glue. With many partitions, other types can lead to worse performance.
question: Which data type should Athena partition keys use?

values.display: partition keys to be of type STRING
push down partition filtering into AWS Glue

qualifiers.condition: the number of partitions is not small

evidence.quote: When you query on partition keys, remember that Athena requires partition keys to be of type STRING in order to push down partition filtering into AWS Glue. If the number of partitions is not small, using other types can lead to worse performance.

claim: If you remove data from a partition in S3, for example with an S3 lifecycle rule, also remove the partition entry from the AWS Glue Data Catalog, because Athena lists every matched partition on S3 during query planning and many empty partitions add overhead.
question: Why remove partition entries after deleting data from S3?

values.display: remove the partition entry from the AWS Glue Data Catalog
If you have many empty partitions

evidence.quote: If you remove data from a partition on Amazon S3 (for example, by using Amazon S3 lifecycle), you should also remove the partition entry from the AWS Glue Data Catalog. During query planning, any partition matched by the query is listed on Amazon S3. If you have many empty partitions, the overhead of listing these partitions can be detrimental.

claim: Queries with equality predicates on all partition keys run faster because the partition metadata can be loaded directly.
question: Which partition filters make Athena queries fastest?

values.display: equality predicates on all partition keys run faster
partition metadata can be loaded directly

evidence.quote: Queries that include equality predicates on all partition keys run faster because the partition metadata can be loaded directly.

claim: MSCK REPAIR TABLE is not an efficient way to manage partitions because it can take a long time, only adds new partitions and does not remove old ones.
question: Why is MSCK REPAIR TABLE a poor partition maintenance tool?

values.display: can take a long time to run
only adds new partitions

evidence.quote: Because MSCK REPAIR TABLE can take a long time to run, only adds new partitions, and does not remove old partitions, it is not an efficient way to manage partitions (see Considerations and limitations).

claim: You can check in advance which partitions an Athena query will scan by prefixing the query with the EXPLAIN statement.
question: How can you see which partitions a query will read before running it?

values.display: by using the EXPLAIN statement
check in advance which partitions a query will scan

evidence.quote: You can check in advance which partitions a query will scan by using the EXPLAIN statement.

claim: Columnar file formats like Parquet and ORC are designed for distributed analytics workloads and organize data by column instead of by row.
question: How do columnar file formats organize data?

values.display: organize data by column instead of by row
designed for distributed analytics workloads

evidence.quote: Columnar file formats like Parquet and ORC are designed for distributed analytics workloads. They organize data by column instead of by row.

claim: With columnar formats only the columns needed for the query are loaded, which reduces the overall amount of data that needs to be loaded.
question: Why do columnar formats scan less data in Athena?

values.display: Only the columns needed for the query are loaded
overall amount of data that needs to be loaded is reduced

evidence.quote: Only the columns needed for the query are loaded
The overall amount of data that needs to be loaded is reduced

claim: Datasets with many small files cause performance issues, particularly with columnar formats, because for small files the overhead of the columnar file format outweighs the benefits.
question: Are small files a problem for Parquet and ORC in Athena?

values.display: datasets with many small files cause performance issues
overhead of the columnar file format outweighs the benefits

evidence.quote: As noted in Avoid having too many files, datasets with many small files cause performance issues. This is particularly true with columnar file formats. For small files, the overhead of the columnar file format outweighs the benefits.

claim: Querying compressed data in Athena is faster and also cheaper, because you pay for the number of bytes scanned before decompression.
question: Does compressing data reduce Athena cost, and why?

values.display: Querying compressed data is faster and also cheaper
bytes scanned before decompression

evidence.quote: Athena supports a wide range of compression formats. Querying compressed data is faster and also cheaper because you pay for the number of bytes scanned before decompression.

claim: Most compression formats require reading a file from the beginning, so compressed text files generally cannot be processed in parallel, while big uncompressed files are often split between workers.
question: Why can compressed CSV or JSON files limit Athena parallelism?

values.display: require the reader to read files from the beginning
compressed text files cannot, in general, be processed in parallel

qualifiers.scope: compressed text files such as JSON and CSV

evidence.quote: Most compression formats require the reader to read files from the beginning. This means that compressed text files cannot, in general, be processed in parallel. Big uncompressed files are often split between workers to achieve higher parallelism during query processing, but this is not possible with most compression formats.

claim: Bucketing distributes records into separate files by the value of a column so that all records with the same value are in the same file. It is useful for a high-cardinality key when many queries look up specific values of that key.
question: When is bucketing useful in Athena?

values.display: distributing records into separate files based on the value of one of the columns
a key with high cardinality

evidence.quote: Bucketing is a technique for distributing records into separate files based on the value of one of the columns. This ensures that all records with the same value will be in the same file. Bucketing is useful when you have a key with high cardinality and many of your queries look up specific values of the key.

claim: Bucketing is less valuable when queries frequently search for multiple values in the bucketed column, because more files may have to be read.
question: When should you avoid bucketing in Athena?

values.display: Bucketing is less valuable
frequently search for multiple values in the column

evidence.quote: Bucketing is less valuable when queries frequently search for multiple values in the column that the data is bucketed by. The more values queried, the higher the likelihood that all or most files will have to be read.

claim: Datasets made of many small files give poor overall query performance because Athena lists all partition locations and each file adds handling and request overhead. Loading a single bigger file from S3 is faster than many smaller files.
question: Why are many small files bad for Athena?

values.display: many small files result in poor overall query performance
loading a single bigger file from Amazon S3 is faster

evidence.quote: Datasets that consist of many small files result in poor overall query performance. When Athena plans a query, it lists all partition locations, which takes time. Handling and requesting each file also has a computational overhead. Therefore, loading a single bigger file from Amazon S3 is faster than loading the same records from many smaller files.

claim: The best time to combine small files is before they are written, for example by writing larger files, using Glue ETL to combine them, or reducing the number of partition keys.
question: How do you fix small files that slow Athena down?

values.display: The best time to combine small files is before they are written
use a tool like Glue ETL to combine them into larger files

evidence.quote: The best time to combine small files is before they are written.
Put files in a location on Amazon S3 and use a tool like Glue ETL to combine them into larger files. Then, move the larger files into the location that the table points to.

claim: To avoid query planning overhead, store files in a flat structure in each partition location, with no additional directory hierarchies.
question: Should files inside an Athena partition be nested in subfolders?

values.display: store files in a flat structure in each partition location
Do not use any additional directory hierarchies

evidence.quote: To avoid query planning overhead, store files in a flat structure in each partition location. Do not use any additional directory hierarchies.

claim: When you use partition projection, include predicates on all partition keys and narrow the possible values to avoid unnecessary S3 listings.
question: What should queries include when a table uses partition projection?

values.display: include predicates on all partition keys
Narrow the scope of possible values

evidence.quote: When you use partition projection, make sure to include predicates on all partition keys. Narrow the scope of possible values to avoid unnecessary Amazon S3 listings.

claim: In an Athena join with an equality condition, the table to the right of JOIN is the build side and must be the smaller table, with the larger table on the left.
question: Which table goes on the right of a JOIN in Athena?

values.display: the right table, the build side, is the smaller of the tables
table to the left of the JOIN keyword is the probe side

evidence.quote: When writing joins with equality-based join conditions, assume that the table to the left of the JOIN keyword is the probe side and the table to the right is the build side. Make sure that the right table, the build side, is the smaller of the tables.

claim: Leave out columns you do not strictly need from an Athena query: less data to process runs faster, and with a columnar format fewer columns also means less data read from S3.
question: Why avoid SELECT * in Athena?

values.display: The less data a query has to process, the faster it will run
reducing the number columns also reduces the amount of data that is read

evidence.quote: If you don't strictly need a column, don't include it in your query. The less data a query has to process, the faster it will run. This reduces both the amount of memory required and the amount of data that has to be sent between nodes. If you are using a columnar file format, reducing the number columns also reduces the amount of data that is read from Amazon S3.

claim: Athena stores a regular query result as a single uncompressed CSV file on S3, which cannot be parallelized. For large results, UNLOAD is usually faster and can write compressed output and other formats such as JSON and Parquet.
question: Why use UNLOAD for large Athena result sets?

values.display: stores the result as a single uncompressed CSV file
UNLOAD writes results directly from the worker nodes

evidence.quote: When a query finishes executing, Athena stores the result as a single uncompressed CSV file on Amazon S3. This takes longer than UNLOAD, not only because the result is uncompressed, but also because the operation cannot be parallelized. In contrast, UNLOAD writes results directly from the worker nodes and makes full use of the parallelism of the compute cluster.

claim: If many queries share the same joins and aggregations, you can materialize the common subquery as a new table with CTAS or Glue ETL and query that table. The disadvantage is that you must keep the new table up to date.
question: How do you speed up queries that repeat the same joins and aggregations in Athena?

values.display: materialize the common subquery as a new table
you must keep the new table up to date

evidence.quote: If many of your queries include the same joins and aggregations, you can materialize the common subquery as a new table and then run queries against that table. You can create the new table with Create a table from query results (CTAS), or a dedicated ETL tool like Glue ETL.
The disadvantage is that you must keep the new table up to date.

claim: You can tell Athena to reuse previously calculated results and specify the maximum age of results to reuse. If the same query ran within that time frame, Athena returns those results instead of running the query again.
question: How does Athena query result reuse work?

values.display: tell Athena to reuse previously calculated results
specify the maximum age of the results to be reused

qualifiers.condition: the same query was run within the maximum age

evidence.quote: When you run a query, you can tell Athena to reuse previously calculated results. You specify the maximum age of the results to be reused. If the same query was previously run within that time frame, Athena returns those results instead of running the query again.
